items.q: What is the main goal of integrated pest management?
options: Keep pests below damaging levels with little pesticide
Kill each pest on a farm with the strongest spray that is sold
Grow crops with no monitoring of the pests in the fields
Replace each pesticide with a stronger one each year

items.q: Releasing ladybugs into a greenhouse to eat aphids is an example of
options: biological control
chemical control
cultural control
a physical barrier

items.q: Why does IPM slow the evolution of pesticide resistance?
options: Spraying less often selects less for resistance
IPM sprays more often, so no pests survive to breed
IPM uses one pesticide each year so pests are unable to adapt
Natural enemies make the pests' genes change back

items.q: Which is a drawback of IPM for a farmer?
options: It takes time, training and labor to monitor pests
It uses more pesticide than spraying on a fixed schedule
It kills more pollinators than ordinary spraying does
It speeds up the evolution of pesticide resistance

items.q: A corn farmer finds that rootworm beetles are a problem each year in fields planted with corn every year. Which IPM step targets the cause?
options: Planting soybeans in alternate years, so the larvae find no corn
Spraying the corn with insecticide each week of the season
Planting the corn a week earlier each year in the same fields
Doubling the fertilizer so that the corn plants outgrow the larvae

items.q: In IPM, why is a pest count below the action threshold not treated, even though some damage occurs?
options: Treating would cost more than the damage and harm natural enemies
Pests below the threshold do no real damage to the crop plants
Pests below the threshold will die out by themselves in a few days
The law forbids treating pests until the threshold is passed

items.q: A farm used 24 kg of insecticide per hectare on a fixed schedule. After switching to IPM, it uses 30% of that amount. How many kilograms per hectare does it use now?

mistakes.why: 16.8 kg is the 70% saved. The farm now uses 30% of the original.
Thirty percent is 0.30, not 30. Multiply 24 by 0.30.

items.q: A school's vegetable garden has aphids. Propose an IPM step (other than spraying a pesticide) and explain how it works.

solution.label: Step
options: release ladybugs or plant flowers that attract them
spray a broad insecticide every week
stop checking the plants

why.1: The question says other than spraying a pesticide.

mechanism.label: How it works
options: eat aphids, a natural predator-prey control
poison the soil so aphids cannot lay eggs
make the plants grow faster than aphids

why.2: Ladybugs do not change plant growth.

effect.label: Result
options: the aphid population stays below a damaging level
the aphids become resistant
the ladybugs eat the vegetables

why.1: Predators do not select for pesticide resistance.

specific.model: The school could release ladybugs or plant flowers that attract them, because ladybugs eat aphids, a natural predator-prey control, so the aphid population stays below a damaging level.

items.q: In which week did the pest count pass the action threshold?
options: Week 5
Week 4
Week 10
Week 1

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in the aphid count from week 5 to week 6, after the targeted control, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: Divide by the starting value, the week 5 count of 12.
Subtract old from new: (6 - 12). The count fell, so the change is negative.
-6 aphids per leaf is the change. Divide by 12 and multiply by 100.
That is the change from week 6 back to week 5. Start from week 5.

items.q: A farm on a fixed schedule sprays every two weeks. How many sprayings would it make in these 10 weeks, compared with the IPM farm's one?
options: 5 sprayings, compared with 1
10 sprayings, compared with 1
2 sprayings, compared with 1
1 spraying, the same as IPM

items.q: In weeks 7 to 10 the count rose again from 4 to 9. What should the IPM farmer do?
options: Keep monitoring and act again if the count passes 10
Spray right away because the count is rising
Stop monitoring because the count is below 10
Release a new pesticide each week to stop the rise

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in insecticide used per hectare from orchard A to orchard B, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: Divide by the starting value, orchard A's 18 kg per ha.
That is B as a percent of A (27.8%). Percent change subtracts first: (5 - 18) / 18 × 100.
-13 kg per ha is the change. Divide by 18 and multiply by 100.
That is the change from B to A. Start from orchard A.

items.q: How much money does orchard B save on pest control across its whole 20 hectares, compared with orchard A?

mistakes.why: 400 dollars is the saving per hectare. Multiply by the 20 hectares.
That is orchard B's total cost. The saving is the difference times 20 ha.

items.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the table?
options: IPM cut spraying and cost, with slightly more damage
IPM raised damaged apples sharply while costing more than spraying
Fixed spraying protected the predatory mites better than IPM did
IPM and fixed spraying used about the same amount of insecticide

items.q: Why might orchard B need fewer sprayings in future seasons as well?
options: Its predatory mites survive and eat the pest mites
Its pests have become resistant, so spraying them is no longer needed
Its apples are damaged more, so pests have less to eat next year
Its insecticide stays on the trees for many seasons after spraying

items.q: Put the steps of an IPM program in a sensible order.
options: Identify the pest and learn its life cycle
Monitor pest numbers regularly
Compare counts with the action threshold
Use biological, physical or cultural controls first
Use a targeted pesticide only if needed, then keep monitoring

items.q: Which practice plants seeds into the leftover stalks of the last crop without plowing?
options: No-till farming
Contour plowing
Terracing
Strip cropping

items.q: How does contour plowing reduce erosion?
options: Rows across the slope hold water back, so less runs downhill
Rows up the slope send water to the bottom of the field faster
Plowing loosens the soil, so it absorbs most of the rain
Contour rows block the wind from reaching the soil

items.q: A farmer rotates corn with soybeans. How does this help the soil?
options: Soybean root bacteria add nitrogen for the next corn crop
Soybeans remove nitrogen from the soil so corn grows taller
Soybeans fill the soil with salt, which corn needs
Soybeans make the soil more acidic so corn roots grow faster

items.q: Farmers on the Great Plains planted rows of trees along their fields after the Dust Bowl. How do these windbreaks protect the soil?
options: They slow the wind near the ground, so less soil blows away
They pull water from deep in the ground and spray it on the field
They add nitrogen to the soil through their roots
They shade the field so that no weeds can grow

items.q: Which is a trade-off of no-till farming?
options: Weeds are often controlled with more herbicide
The soil erodes faster than it did before
Soil organic matter falls quickly
More fuel is burned by the tractors

items.q: A farm in steep mountains has thin soil that washes away after heavy rains. Which practice fits the land best?
options: Terracing, cutting the slopes into flat steps
Windbreaks along the field edges to stop wind erosion
Plowing straight up and down the slope to drain the water
Adding more synthetic fertilizer to replace lost nutrients

items.q: A 40-hectare field loses 18 metric tons of soil per hectare each year. After switching to no-till it loses 3 metric tons per hectare. How many metric tons of soil does the field save each year?

mistakes.why: 15 metric tons is the saving for one hectare. Multiply by the 40 hectares.
120 metric tons is what the field still loses. The saving is (18 - 3) × 40.

items.q: Soil on a sloping cornfield is washing into a stream. Propose a soil conservation practice for the farm and explain how it works.

solution.label: Practice
options: plant alternating strips of corn and hay across the slope
plow up and down the slope
remove all crop residue after harvest

why.1: Up-and-down rows channel water downhill and speed erosion.

mechanism.label: How it works
options: the dense hay strips slow runoff and trap soil washed from the corn strips
the hay strips speed water to the stream
the corn strips absorb soil from the stream

why.1: Dense strips slow water, not speed it.
why.2: Crops do not take soil out of streams.

effect.label: Result
options: less soil reaches the stream
more soil reaches the stream
the stream dries up

why.2: Strip cropping does not dry up streams.

specific.model: The farmer could plant alternating strips of corn and hay across the slope, which slows runoff because the dense hay strips trap soil washed from the corn strips, so less soil reaches the stream.

items.q: In the left panel of the diagram, which way do the plowed rows run?
options: Across the slope, along the contour
Straight up and down the slope
In circles around a central well
On the flat ground at the bottom of the hill

items.q: According to the right panel, why does terracing reduce erosion?
options: Water pools on each flat step and soaks in
The steps are steeper than the original slope, so water drains faster
The steps are built of rock, so they do not hold any soil
The steps catch wind and keep it from reaching the crop

items.q: Which situation fits the left panel's practices better than the right panel's?
options: A gently rolling field worked by machines
A very steep mountainside with thin soil
A flat desert field with strong winds
A flooded rice paddy on a river delta

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in soil lost from plowing up and down the slope to no-till with contour rows, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: Divide by the starting value, 20 metric tons per ha.
Subtract old from new: (2 - 20). Soil loss fell, so the change is negative.
-18 metric tons per ha is the change. Divide by 20 and multiply by 100.
Soil loss fell, so the percent change is negative: -90%.

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in corn yield from plowing up and down the slope to contour plowing with strip cropping, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: Divide by the starting value, 9.6.
That is the change in metric tons per ha (-0.4). Divide by 9.6 and multiply by 100.
-0.4 metric tons per ha is the change. Divide by 9.6 and multiply by 100.
That is the change from strip cropping back to up-and-down plowing. Start from up-and-down.

items.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the table?
options: Conservation practices cut soil loss with small yield drops
Conservation practices cut yield in half while saving little soil
Plowing up and down the slope gave the least soil loss of the four
Soil loss and yield were about the same under each practice

items.q: Topsoil forms at roughly 1 metric ton per hectare per year. Which practice in the table comes closest to keeping soil loss at that rate?
options: No-till with contour rows, losing 2 metric tons per ha per year
Contour plowing alone, losing 10 metric tons per ha per year
Contour plowing with strip cropping, losing 5 metric tons per ha per year
Plowing up and down the slope, losing 20 metric tons per ha per year

items.q: Which practices add organic matter or nutrients to farm soil? Select all that apply.
options: Spreading manure or compost
Growing clover or another legume in rotation
Leaving crop residue on the field (no-till)
Plowing the field twice a year
Burning crop residue after harvest
Removing the plant material from the field

items.q: Which is an example of aquaculture?
options: Raising salmon in net pens in a bay
Catching tuna with longlines at sea
Trawling the sea floor for shrimp
Fishing for trout with a rod in a river

items.q: Which is a benefit of aquaculture compared with wild fishing?
options: It grows a lot of food on little space
It removes the need to give the fish any feed
It is unable to spread disease to any wild fish
It produces no waste in the water

items.q: Waste from a crowded salmon pen collects on the sea floor below it. Why does the water near the bottom lose oxygen?
options: Decomposers use up oxygen breaking down waste
The waste blocks sunlight, so the sea floor heats up
The salmon breathe in the oxygen from the sea floor
The waste turns the salt water into fresh water

items.q: Farmed salmon in net pens often carry sea lice, a parasite. Why is this a concern for wild salmon?
options: Young wild salmon swimming past can get lice
Sea lice from the pens make the wild salmon grow faster
Sea lice eat the waste under the pens and clean the water
Sea lice live on farmed salmon and stay inside the pens

items.q: Why does farming salmon do less to reduce pressure on wild fish than farming tilapia?
options: Salmon feed is made partly from wild fish
Salmon grow faster than tilapia, so more of them are farmed
Tilapia escape more often, so they replace wild fish in the sea
Salmon are farmed on land while tilapia are farmed in the sea

items.q: In parts of Southeast Asia, coastal shrimp farms were built by clearing mangrove forests. Which is a likely result?
options: Coasts lose storm protection and fish nurseries
Coasts gain storm protection because the ponds block waves
Wild fish catches rise because shrimp ponds feed them
Mangroves grow back inside the ponds within a year

items.q: A fish farm produces 1,200 metric tons of salmon. It takes about 1.3 kg of feed to grow 1 kg of salmon. How many metric tons of feed does the farm use?

mistakes.why: It takes 1.3 kg of feed per kilogram of fish, so multiply by 1.3.
A factor of 10 slipped: 1,200 × 1.3 = 1,560.

items.q: A town wants a fish farm in its bay but worries about pollution. Propose a farming method that would limit the harm and explain how it works.

solution.label: Method
options: raise the fish in closed tanks on land with filters
double the number of fish in each net pen
feed the fish more often in open pens

why.1: More crowding means more waste and disease.
why.2: More feed means more uneaten feed falling to the bottom.

mechanism.label: How it works
options: filters capture waste and the water is cleaned and reused
waste flows straight into the bay
wild fish eat all the waste

why.1: That is the problem the town wants to avoid.
why.2: Wild fish do not remove concentrated waste.

effect.label: Result
options: little waste reaches the bay and farmed fish cannot escape into it
more waste reaches the bay
the bay loses oxygen faster

why.1: Closed tanks keep waste out of the bay.
why.2: Less waste means less oxygen loss.

specific.model: The town could raise the fish in closed tanks on land with filters, which capture waste so the water is cleaned and reused. As a result little waste reaches the bay and farmed fish cannot escape into it.

items.q: In the diagram, what happens to waste and uneaten feed from the open net pen?
options: It sinks to the sea floor below the pen
It passes through a filter and is reused
It is eaten by the escaped fish
It floats to the surface and evaporates

items.q: Which problem shown for the open pen is solved by the closed tank design?
options: Farmed fish escaping into the wild
The cost of electricity for pumps
The need to feed the fish
The need to clean the water

items.q: Why are many fish farms still built as open pens even though closed tanks cause less pollution?
options: Open pens cost much less to build and run
Open pens produce no waste in the water
Closed tanks are unable to hold saltwater fish
Closed tanks spread more disease to wild fish

items.q: Which trend does the table show from 1990 to 2022?
options: Aquaculture grew to 95 while wild capture stayed near 90
Wild capture grew from 85 to 95 million metric tons while aquaculture fell
Both wild capture and aquaculture fell between 1990 and 2022
Aquaculture stayed near 15 while wild capture grew to 95

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in aquaculture production from 2000 to 2022, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: Divide by the starting value, the 2000 production of 35.
That is 2022 as a percent of 2000 (271%). Percent change subtracts first.
60 million metric tons is the change. Divide by 35 and multiply by 100.
That is the change from 2022 back to 2000. Start from 2000.

items.q: In 2022, what percent of total production (wild capture plus aquaculture) came from aquaculture?

mistakes.why: Divide by the total, 90 + 95 = 185, not by wild capture alone.
48.6% is the share from wild capture. Aquaculture is 95 of 185.

items.q: In the table, wild capture has stayed near 90 million metric tons since 1990 while demand for fish grew. What does this suggest?
options: Wild fisheries are near their limit, so farming met the new demand
Wild fisheries could easily double their catch if more boats were built
Demand for fish has fallen, so farms are producing more than needed
Fish farming has caused wild fish stocks to grow much larger

items.q: Which are drawbacks of open net-pen fish farming? Select all that apply.
options: Waste and uneaten feed pollute the water below the pens
Disease and parasites spread to wild fish
Farmed fish escape and compete with wild fish
Pens produce more bycatch than trawling
Pens raise the oxygen level of the bay
Pens use more fuel than fishing fleets

items.q: Which forestry method harvests some trees and leaves most of the forest standing?
options: Selective cutting
Clearcutting
Prescribed burning
Slash-and-burn

items.q: Why does selective cutting cause less erosion than clearcutting?
options: Most trees stay, so roots hold the soil
The cut trees are left on the ground to block the stream
Selective cutting is done in winter, when there is no rain
The soil under selected trees is harder, so it does not move

items.q: How does a prescribed burn reduce the harm from later wildfires?
options: It burns brush, so later fires have less fuel
It kills the large trees, so wildfires have nothing tall to burn
It adds moisture to the soil, so the forest is unable to burn
It leaves ash that blocks oxygen from reaching future fires

items.q: Which is a drawback of selective cutting compared with clearcutting?
options: It costs more per log to harvest
It causes more erosion because the soil is left bare
It removes more habitat for forest animals
It makes streams warmer by removing the shade over them

items.q: A company replaces a cut native mixed forest with a plantation of one fast-growing pine species. Compared with regrowing the native forest, which is a likely cost?
options: Lower biodiversity, as one tree species supports fewer animals
Lower wood production, because pines grow slowly
More soil erosion, because pines have no roots
More shade on streams, because pines are taller

items.q: Which action by a family most directly lowers the demand for cutting trees?
options: Buying recycled paper and reclaimed wood
Buying more new paper products made from fresh wood
Burning wood in a fireplace instead of using gas heat
Replacing wooden fences with new ones each other year

items.q: A 5,000-hectare forest grows 4 m³ of new wood per hectare each year. To harvest sustainably, how many cubic meters of wood can be cut each year at most?

mistakes.why: Multiply the area by the growth per hectare so the hectares cancel.
4 m³ is the growth on one hectare. Multiply by the 5,000 hectares.

items.q: A logging company wants to harvest timber from a forested hillside above a trout stream. Propose a forestry method and explain how it protects the stream.

solution.label: Method
options: cut selected trees and leave a strip of forest along the stream
clearcut the whole hillside down to the water
burn the hillside before logging

why.1: Clearcutting to the water bares soil and removes shade.
why.2: Burning before logging bares the soil.

mechanism.label: How it works
options: keeps roots holding the soil and shade over the stream
removes the trees that shade the stream
adds sediment to the stream bed

effect.label: Result
options: less sediment reaches the stream and the water stays cool for trout
more sediment reaches the stream
the stream warms and loses oxygen

specific.model: The company could cut selected trees and leave a strip of forest along the stream, which keeps roots holding the soil and shade over the stream. As a result less sediment reaches the stream and the water stays cool for trout.

items.q: In the reforestation panel, what is shown?
options: Rows of seedlings planted on cut land
A few mature trees cut from a standing forest
A low fire burning brush under large trees
Large trees standing with no young trees

items.q: In the prescribed burn panel, why do the large trees survive the fire?
options: The fire is low, below the large trees' crowns
The large trees are cut down before the fire is set
The fire is set in the treetops, away from the trunks
The large trees are sprayed with water by the fire crew

items.q: Which panel's practice best matches the idea of maximum sustainable yield?
options: Selective cutting, matched to the yearly growth
Prescribed burn, because it produces the most timber
Reforestation, because seedlings can be harvested in a year
Neither, because sustainable yield applies to fish and not trees

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in fuel on the forest floor from the unburned plots to the plots with prescribed burns, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: Divide by the starting value, 40 metric tons per ha in the unburned plots.
That is the burned plots as a percent of the unburned (20%). Percent change subtracts first.
-32 metric tons per ha is the change. Divide by 40 and multiply by 100.
20% is how much fuel was left. The percent change is -80%.

items.q: How many times higher were the flames in plots without prescribed burns than in plots with them?

mistakes.why: Put the unburned plots' flame height (12 m) on top.
Subtracting gives the difference in meters. Divide to find how many times higher.

items.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the table?
options: Less fuel led to lower flames and fewer large trees killed
More fuel on the floor led to lower flames and fewer large trees killed
Prescribed burns killed more large trees than the wildfire did
Flame height had no link to the number of large trees killed

items.q: A town sits next to the unburned forest. What does the table suggest the town should support?
options: Prescribed burns or fuel removal near the town
Putting out each small fire, so fuel keeps building on the floor
Planting more brush near homes to block the wind
Removing the large trees and leaving the brush behind

items.q: Put the steps of a sustainable selective harvest in a sensible order.
options: Survey the forest and measure how much wood it grows each year
Mark mature trees to cut, keeping strips along streams
Cut and haul out only the marked trees
Replant or let seedlings regrow in the gaps, then monitor
